Fare
fār
v. and n. (to go, to travel, to be in a condition; and the price paid for passage)
Saxon faran, to go or travel — the root still visible in wayfaring, welfare and farewell. Both biblical senses descend from it: to fare is to go on, and a fare is what you pay to be carried.

Biblical Definition

Jesse sends David to the camp with ten cheeses for the captain and one errand: “look how thy brethren fare, and take their pledge” (1Sa 17:18) — go and see how they do. That is the old sense of the verb: not what a man eats but how he goes on. It is the errand of an ordinary son on an ordinary morning, and it puts him in the valley when Goliath comes out. The noun is Jonah's, and it is one of the saddest details in the prophets: “he found a ship going to Tarshish: so he paid the fare thereof, and went down into it, to go with them unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD” (Jon 1:3). Flight from God costs money. There was a ship, there was an opening, there was a price he could afford — and none of that made it providence approving his errand. Three times in the verse he goes down: down to Joppa, down into the ship, and later down into the sides of the vessel and down to the bottoms of the mountains. The last use is the ordinary courtesy at the end of the Jerusalem letter: “from which if ye keep yourselves, ye shall do well. Fare ye well” (Act 15:29) — go well, travel well, be in good case.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines fare as to go, to pass, to travel; to be in any state, good or ill; and as a noun, the price of passage, or food provided.

expand to see more

FARE, v.i. To go; to pass; to move forward; to travel.

1. To be in any state, good or bad; to be attended with any circumstances or train of events, fortunate or unfortunate.

FARE, n. The price of passage, or the sum paid or due for conveying a person by land or water.

1. Food; provisions of the table.

Key Scripture

Jon 1:3 — "But Jonah rose up to flee unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD, and went down to Joppa; and he found a ship going to Tarshish: so he paid the fare thereof, and went down into it, to go with them unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD."

1Sa 17:18 — "And carry these ten cheeses unto the captain of their thousand, and look how thy brethren fare, and take their pledge."

Act 15:29 — "That ye abstain from meats offered to idols, and from blood, and from things strangled, and from fornication: from which if ye keep yourselves, ye shall do well. Fare ye well."

Modern Corruption

An open door is treated as divine approval; Jonah found a ship, and it was sailing away from God.

expand to see more

A whole style of guidance rests on circumstance: the door opened, the ticket was available, the timing worked, therefore God must be in it. Jonah 1:3 is the standing refutation. There was a ship at Joppa going exactly where he wanted to go, and he could pay the fare, and every one of those facts was true while he was fleeing the presence of the LORD. Providence arranges the means of a rebellion as surely as the means of an obedience, and it does so without endorsing either. The revealed will of God in His word, not the alignment of circumstance, is what tells a man where he ought to be.

The other half of the picture is Jesse's errand. David was sent to see how his brothers fared and to bring back a token, and that unremarkable obedience placed him in the valley of Elah on the day Israel needed a champion. God's great turns are usually reached through small assigned duties rather than through discerned destinies. The man who wants to know God's will for his life will generally find it lying in the errand his father gave him this morning.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shalom (H7965), peace, welfare, how one does; sakar (H7939), hire, wages, fare; Greek rhonnumi (G4517), to be strong — the farewell formula.

expand to see more

Hebrew shalom (H7965) — peace, soundness, welfare; 1 Samuel 17:18, literally look to the peace of thy brethren.

Hebrew sakar (H7939) — hire, wages, the price paid; Jonah 1:3, the fare of the ship.

Hebrew yarad (H3381) — to go down; used three times of Jonah's flight — down to Joppa, down into the ship, down into the sides.

Hebrew 'arubbah (H6161) — a pledge, a token; the pledge David was to bring back.

Greek rhonnumi (G4517) — to be strong, to fare well; Acts 15:29, the closing word of the Jerusalem letter.

Usage

"“Look how thy brethren fare” — an errand that ended in a valley."

"“So he paid the fare thereof” — and the ship was real, and the flight was sin."

"“Fare ye well” — the letter's last word to the Gentile churches."
